claims.text: Multiphase refractory high-entropy alloys can exhibit a ductile-brittle-ductile transition during isothermal aging.
Positive mixing enthalpies between constituent elements are a boundary condition for the proposed non-monotonic ductility transition.
The sequential formation and subsequent dissolution of brittle B2 or Heusler ordering drives the proposed ductility transition.
The relevant initial microstructure contains BCC solid solutions together with incipient precipitates.
The Fe-Cr pair has a positive mixing enthalpy that provides a driving force for precipitation.
Positive Al-Nb mixing enthalpy drives phase separation in the proposed refractory alloy systems.
Aging at 700–1000 °C over short to long durations induces chemical ordering and phase evolution.
The aging temperature must overcome kinetic barriers to ordering while remaining below the solvus for complete dissolution of the ordered phase.
Initially nucleated B2 or Heusler-type ordered phases are brittle and cause embrittlement.
Coarsening or dissolution of the ordered phases restores ductility.
Positive mixing enthalpies drive short-range and long-range chemical ordering in Al1.5CoCrFeNi.
Short-range and long-range ordering restrict dislocation motion and cause brittleness.
At extended aging times, ordered phases dissolve or become incoherent through coarsening and therefore impede slip less severely.
Elongation to failure versus aging time will follow a U-shaped or V-shaped curve, potentially recovering to or exceeding the initial ductility.
Many conventionally aged alloys show monotonic ductility degradation associated with precipitation hardening and embrittlement.
The transition will not occur in alloys dominated by solid-solution strengthening or containing an indefinitely stable ordered phase.
The time and temperature windows for ductility recovery in Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr are uncertain because its phase stability and transformations are insufficiently established.
Creep or oxidation could mask a recovery in ductility during long-term aging.
The proposed experiment measures tensile elongation and ordered-phase characteristics across aging times from 1 to 10,000 hours at 800 °C.
A monotonic ductility curve or absence of correlation between the ductility minimum and peak ordered-phase fraction falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prescribed aging temperature is stated to remain below the solvus for complete dissolution, while recovery is repeatedly attributed to subsequent dissolution of the ordered phase during aging. The hypothesis does not explain how dissolution occurs under the stated below-solvus boundary.
